scenes.heading: Coalesce
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Coalesce and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What coalesce does
items: Avoids a full shuffle by merging locally
scenes.narration: Coalesce lowers the partition count by merging existing partitions on the same executors rather than reshuffling all the data. Because it avoids network movement, it is far cheaper than repartition when you only need fewer partitions. Its most common use is trimming output down to a sensible number of files before a write.

scenes.heading: How merging works
scenes.narration: Coalesce works by collapsing several existing partitions into one wherever it can do so on the same node. Since it minimizes data movement across the network, the operation is narrow in most cases. The trade-off is that the resulting partitions can be uneven, because it does not rebalance rows, only combines them.

scenes.code:
result = (spark.read.parquet("/data/logs")
              .filter("level = 'ERROR'")
              .coalesce(1))
result.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/out/errors")
# Writes a single file instead of hundreds of tiny ones
scenes.heading: Preventing small files on write
scenes.narration: After filtering, most partitions may hold only a handful of error rows, which would otherwise produce hundreds of tiny output files. Coalescing to one merges them so the write emits a single file. Be careful with coalesce to one on very large data, though, because it funnels everything through a single task and can bottleneck or run out of memory.

scenes.heading: When to pick which
scenes.narration: Choose coalesce when you are shrinking partition counts and want to avoid the shuffle, especially right before writing. Choose repartition when you need to grow parallelism, want evenly balanced partitions, or must partition by a key. Matching the tool to the goal is the difference between a cheap tweak and an expensive shuffle.

scenes.text: Coalesce to trim files; repartition to rebalance work.
scenes.narration: Reaching for coalesce on the write side is one of the simplest fixes for the small-files problem.
